prize_parts.citation: For an oeuvre that remakes the boundaries of lyric, essay and narrative in dialogue with antiquity, and gives grief and desire new formal shape.

statement.case_for: Carson's voice is hard to mistake for anyone else's. On public knowledge, Autobiography of Red recasts a fragmentary Greek source as a modern verse novel, and Nox turns elegy into a material object built around loss. Her essays and her work with classical sources, which I understand to include translation, carry the same project into other forms. The formal invention does not stand apart from the subject matter. The hybrid form is how the work handles grief, desire and the distance of ancient texts. That puts her strongly on distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, and imaginative and intellectual depth. She writes in English, so for the text itself there is no translation loss to discount, though the visual and material side of her books is hard to judge from description. Her publishing across several decades suggests a sustained, evolving practice rather than a single breakthrough. I am relying on public knowledge, not fresh reading, and I have not independently verified the texts.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Mattson and Carlberg also raise: how much of the corpus is original creation and how much is translation, adaptation or scholarship. The hybrid forms also make it harder to name one central achievement than for Cărtărescu, whose project is more legible as a single architecture. Whether the book-object works will last in the canon, rather than staying influential among writers, is a judgment I cannot settle from the supplied evidence. If the committee reads her breadth as diffusion rather than range, this case weakens.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson third. She finds Carson's originality real but the range of modes makes a single central achievement hard to define. She adds that translations and versions of classical texts are partly derivative and must be separated from original work, and that the weight of the canonical works is still debated.
responses.response: I accept the need to separate the translations and versions from the original work, and I would want the citation to rest on the original books and essays, not on the classical renderings. I do not agree that the range of modes obscures the central achievement. In the works I know best, the shared move is a fragmentary or inherited source reworked until its form carries an emotional argument. That is a unifying method, not diffusion. I concede the point about canonical weight: it is still open and a committee should say so openly.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He credits Cărtărescu with a large inner world built through linguistic and structural invention. He asks whether Carson's genre-crossing work fits the will's wording on an idealistic direction, and whether the weight placed on that wording needs discussion.
responses.response: The question about the will is fair, and I do not think Carson's work is exempt from it. I would read the idealistic direction as seriousness of purpose and intellectual and emotional depth. On that reading, her sustained attention to loss, desire and how ancient texts keep speaking fits well. I also agree that Cărtărescu's scale is formidable, and that the case for him rests on the whole oeuvre. Our difference is partly one of weighting: I put more value on formal economy and the force of compressed lyric invention, while Olsson seems to put more on the coherence of a large cosmology. I do not think genre classification counts against Carson in itself.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg gives Carson first place but warns that her scholarly and classical allusiveness may narrow the readership the Academy would regard as essential. He also asks whether the hybrid books outweigh a more conventionally narrative or poetic body of work.
responses.response: I share the concern, but I would not treat breadth of readership as a criterion in itself, and a demanding source base is not a defect. I also think the allusiveness is less closed than it might seem. As I understand Nox, the emotional matter of the elegy is available without specialist knowledge, and the classical apparatus adds to it rather than gating it. On his second question, I would not set the hybrid books against a conventional body of work, because the lyric and narrative strengths appear within the hybrid forms. That is a claim from public knowledge, though, and close reading by the committee would test it.

uncertainties: My knowledge of Carson's later and more performance-oriented work is secondhand, so whether recent output matches the earlier peaks is unresolved.
The boundary between original work and translation or adaptation in the corpus needs agreed handling before a citation is drafted.
The material and visual dimensions of her books cannot be fully assessed from descriptions, so a text-only reading may understate or distort them.
For Cărtărescu, the main alternative, I cannot judge how far translation preserves the density of the Romanian prose, which limits any direct comparison.
For Tawada, the other alternative, her wordplay across Japanese and German is only partly accessible in translation, and the two-language scope complicates the citation.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile: it records no personal, institutional or collaborative connection to any shortlisted writer. My own writing on art, creativity and women's lives is context, not evidence of preference, and I do not treat it as a reason for or against any candidate.
